title: CPU Upgrade Path
overview: A CPU upgrade is a socket-and-chipset puzzle: the new chip must fit your motherboard’s socket AND be supported by its chipset/BIOS. Get those two right and it is a 20-minute swap with big gains; get them wrong and you own an expensive paperweight.

demo.how_to_run: python checker.py  — edit the YOUR BUILD section with your parts

compatibility_checks: Socket must match exactly (e.g. AM4, LGA1700, AM5 — they are not interchangeable)
Chipset must support the chip (check the motherboard vendor’s CPU support list)
BIOS version must be new enough — update BIOS BEFORE swapping on older boards
Cooler must handle the new TDP; check mounting-kit compatibility
PSU headroom for higher-TDP chips
bottleneck_notes: CPU-bound signs: 100% CPU in Task Manager while GPU idles in games; slow renders/encodes. If the GPU is already at 100%, a CPU upgrade helps little.
steps: Identify your motherboard model and current BIOS version
Look up the vendor CPU support list; pick a chip on it
Update BIOS to the required version with the OLD CPU still installed
Power off, unplug, remove cooler, release the socket lever
Lift old CPU straight up (never force); note the triangle alignment marker
Drop new CPU in by the triangle, close lever, clean and repaste, remount cooler
Boot to BIOS: verify the new CPU is detected and temps are sane
warning: Bent socket pins are usually fatal — lower the CPU vertically, zero force.
provenance: Standard PC upgrade procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: GPU Upgrade Path
overview: GPU upgrades are the most common gaming upgrade. The checks: physical fit in the case, PSU wattage and power connectors, PCIe slot version (mostly backward compatible), and monitor resolution — a 4K card on a 1080p/60Hz monitor is wasted.

demo.how_to_run: python checker.py  — edit the YOUR BUILD section with your parts

compatibility_checks: Card length vs case GPU clearance (measure!)
PSU wattage: GPU TDP + system, keep 40%+ headroom
Correct PCIe power cables: 6-pin, 8-pin, or 12VHPWR — adapters exist but native is better
PCIe x16 slot available; gen 3/4/5 interoperate
Monitor resolution/refresh should justify the card
bottleneck_notes: GPU-bound signs: GPU at 95-100% in games while CPU idles. Check with MSI Afterburner overlay. CPU bottlenecks show as low GPU usage.
steps: Uninstall old GPU driver with DDU in Safe Mode (recommended)
Power off, unplug, remove old card (release PCIe latch!)
Seat new card until the latch clicks; connect ALL power cables
Boot, install the latest driver from NVIDIA/AMD/Intel
Verify: Device Manager shows the card; run a benchmark; check temps under load
warning: The PCIe slot latch must be released before pulling the old card — ripped slots are a classic injury.
provenance: Standard PC upgrade procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: RAM Upgrade and XMP
overview: RAM upgrades are cheap and easy — when RAM is actually the limit. Match the DDR generation to your board, prefer matched kits, and enable XMP/DOCP afterward or you leave 20-40% performance on the table.

demo.how_to_run: python checker.py  — edit the YOUR BUILD section with your parts

compatibility_checks: DDR generation must match the board (DDR4 vs DDR5 — different slots)
Prefer a matched kit over mixing brands/speeds
Check max capacity per slot in the manual
Laptops: verify RAM is not soldered
bottleneck_notes: RAM-bound signs: high "Committed" memory in Task Manager, disk thrashing with free CPU. 16 GB is the 2026 sweet spot; 8 GB is minimum.
steps: Buy a matched kit (2 sticks) of the board’s DDR generation
Power off, unplug, open case
Install in the recommended slots (usually A2/B2 — 2nd and 4th from CPU)
Press firmly until BOTH clips snap
Boot to BIOS: enable XMP/DOCP/EXPO
Verify in Task Manager > Memory: speed matches the box; run a memory test
warning: Ground yourself on the case. Never force — the notch must align.
provenance: Standard PC upgrade procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: SATA SSD Upgrade
overview: Any 2.5" SATA SSD drops into any PC from the last 15 years and transforms it. The only checks: a free SATA port and a mounting spot (or adapter bracket).

demo.how_to_run: python checker.py  — edit the YOUR BUILD section with your parts

compatibility_checks: Free SATA data port on the motherboard
SATA power lead from the PSU
2.5" bay or adapter bracket
SATA mode AHCI in BIOS (not IDE)
bottleneck_notes: If Task Manager shows 100% disk on an HDD, this is THE upgrade. Even a budget SATA SSD is 5-10x faster in real use.
steps: Connect the SSD (data + power) or use a USB cloning dock
Clone with the vendor’s free tool, or clean-install Windows
Set the SSD first in BIOS boot order
Verify it boots; keep the HDD as data storage
Enable TRIM (automatic in Windows): fsutil behavior query DisableDeleteNotify should be 0
warning: Verify the clone boots before wiping the old drive.
provenance: Standard PC upgrade procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: NVMe M.2 SSD Install
overview: NVMe drives are 5-10x faster than SATA SSDs and slot directly into the motherboard — no cables. Check: M.2 slot keying (M-key for NVMe), length (2280 standard), and whether the slot is SATA-only on old boards.

demo.how_to_run: python checker.py  — edit the YOUR BUILD section with your parts

compatibility_checks: M.2 slot present and NVMe-capable (check manual — some M.2 slots are SATA-only)
Length: 2280 is standard; 22110 needs a longer slot
Heatsink: motherboard armor or the drive’s own — Gen4/5 drives throttle without one
Standoff and screw present (often in the motherboard box)
bottleneck_notes: NVMe shines in large file work and game loading; for basic desktop use the jump from SATA SSD is smaller than HDD-to-SSD was.
steps: Power off, unplug; locate the M.2 slot (often under a heatsink plate)
Insert the drive at ~30 degrees, press down, secure with standoff screw
Replace heatsink plate (remove its film!)
Boot: the drive appears in BIOS storage info
Initialize in Disk Management (GPT), format, or clone Windows onto it
warning: Remove the plastic film from heatsink thermal pads. Do not overtighten the tiny screw.
provenance: Standard PC upgrade procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: PSU Upgrade and Wattage Math
overview: The PSU powers everything and protects it. Size it: sum TDPs, add 40% headroom, buy 80+ Bronze minimum (Gold preferred), and never cheap out — a bad PSU can kill every other part.

demo.how_to_run: python checker.py  — edit the YOUR BUILD section with your parts

compatibility_checks: Wattage: (CPU TDP + GPU TDP + 150W) x 1.4 = target
ATX size fits the case (SFX for small cases)
Correct cables: 24-pin, 8-pin CPU, PCIe 6+2 or 12VHPWR for the GPU
80+ rating: Bronze minimum, Gold sweet spot
Modular vs non-modular (cable management)
bottleneck_notes: PSU "bottlenecks" show as random shutdowns/reboots under load, or coil whine. Undersized PSUs cause exactly the symptoms of other failing parts.
steps: Calculate target wattage with the checker below
Buy reputable (Seasonic, Corsair, EVGA, be quiet!) with 7-10yr warranty
Photo the old cable routing before removing
Power off, unplug, hold power 10s to drain
Swap PSU; route 24-pin, CPU 8-pin, and PCIe cables first
NEVER reuse modular cables from a different PSU brand/model — pinouts differ and can fry parts
Boot and stress-test
warning: Modular cable pinouts are NOT standardized — mixing brands kills hardware. Never open a PSU.
provenance: Standard PC upgrade procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Motherboard Swap
overview: A motherboard swap is essentially a rebuild: new board means verifying CPU socket, RAM generation, and case form factor (ATX/mATX/ITX) all at once. Plan for a Windows reactivation and driver refresh.

demo.how_to_run: python checker.py  — edit the YOUR BUILD section with your parts

compatibility_checks: Socket matches your CPU (or you are upgrading CPU too)
RAM generation matches your sticks (DDR4 vs DDR5)
Form factor fits the case (ATX board needs ATX case)
Enough fan headers, M.2 slots, USB ports for your parts
BIOS supports your CPU out of the box (or has BIOS flashback)
bottleneck_notes: Motherboards rarely bottleneck speed — they bottleneck FEATURES: PCIe lanes, USB count, VRM quality for high-TDP CPUs, overclocking support.
steps: Photo everything: cable routing, front-panel connectors
Remove GPU, cooler, RAM, drives, then the old board
Install CPU/RAM/M.2 on the new board BEFORE mounting (easier)
Mount standoffs correctly for the form factor — extra standoffs short the board
Connect 24-pin, 8-pin CPU, front panel (use the manual diagram)
Boot: enter BIOS, set boot order, enable XMP
Windows: reactivate license (link to Microsoft account first); install chipset drivers
warning: Standoff shorts kill boards — verify each standoff aligns with a mounting hole.
provenance: Standard PC upgrade procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Case Airflow and Fan Upgrades
overview: Good airflow is free performance: cool components do not throttle. The formula is simple — intake front/bottom, exhaust rear/top, clear paths, dust filters maintained.

demo.how_to_run: python checker.py  — edit the YOUR BUILD section with your parts

compatibility_checks: Fan sizes the case supports (120mm/140mm per mount)
Enough SYS_FAN headers (or a hub/splitter)
Clearance: tall air coolers vs side panel
Positive pressure (more intake) reduces dust
bottleneck_notes: Airflow "bottlenecks" are thermal: components throttle when hot. If temps drop 10C with the side panel off, airflow is the problem.
steps: Map current fans: which are intake vs exhaust (blades curve toward airflow)
Add intake fans front/bottom, exhaust rear/top
Route cables behind the motherboard tray
Set fan curves in BIOS (ramp with CPU temp)
Clean dust filters monthly
Retest temps under load
warning: None — the safest upgrade there is.
provenance: Standard PC upgrade procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: AIO Liquid Cooler Install
overview: All-in-one liquid coolers handle high-TDP CPUs quietly. The keys: radiator fits the case, pump header powered, and tubes routed without kinks — radiator ABOVE the pump to avoid airlock.

demo.how_to_run: python checker.py  — edit the YOUR BUILD section with your parts

compatibility_checks: Radiator size fits case mounts (240/280/360mm)
Socket bracket included for your socket (AM4/AM5/LGA1700)
Pump/AIO header on motherboard (or SATA power)
Case clearance for radiator + fans thickness
bottleneck_notes: AIOs help sustained all-core loads (rendering, compiling). For gaming on mid CPUs, a good air cooler matches them cheaper.
steps: Mount the backplate for your socket
Apply paste (pea dot) or use pre-applied
Seat the pump block evenly; tighten in an X pattern
Mount radiator with tubes at the BOTTOM if front-mounted (avoids air in pump)
Connect pump to AIO_PUMP header, fans to CPU_FAN
Boot: verify pump RPM in BIOS (~2000-3000); check temps
warning: Radiator below the pump traps air in the pump and kills it early. Tubes down on front mounts.
provenance: Standard PC upgrade procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Thermal Paste Replacement
overview: Paste dries out in 2-4 years, and temperatures creep up. Repasting is a $10 maintenance upgrade: clean, pea-sized dot, remount evenly.

demo.how_to_run: python checker.py  — edit the YOUR BUILD section with your parts

compatibility_checks: Paste type: standard ceramic/metal is fine; liquid metal is expert-only
Cooler mounting hardware intact
Isopropyl alcohol 90%+ for cleaning
bottleneck_notes: Repaste when load temps rose 10C+ since new with the same cooler. It restores lost thermal headroom, not magic speed.
steps: Power off, unplug; remove the cooler (twist gently if stuck)
Clean CPU and cooler base with isopropyl + lint-free cloth
Pea-sized dot (rice grain for small dies) center of the CPU
Remount cooler with even pressure (X-pattern screws)
Boot and compare temps to before
warning: Liquid metal conducts electricity — one drop in the wrong place kills the board. Beginners: use normal paste.
provenance: Standard PC upgrade procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Wi-Fi 6/7 Card Upgrade
overview: A $25 Wi-Fi card upgrade (Intel AX210/BE200) fixes old laptops/desktops stuck on slow Wi-Fi. Check: M.2 E-key or PCIe slot, and antenna connectors.

demo.how_to_run: python checker.py  — edit the YOUR BUILD section with your parts

compatibility_checks: Slot: M.2 2230 E-key (laptops) or PCIe x1 (desktops)
Antenna leads present (laptops have them; desktops need antennas)
Driver support for your Windows version
Router should support Wi-Fi 6/7 to see full gains
bottleneck_notes: Wi-Fi card upgrades help only if the old card was the limit — test wired speed first. Old 1x1 802.11n cards are the classic culprit.
steps: Buy Intel AX210 (Wi-Fi 6E) or BE200 (Wi-Fi 7) in the right form factor
Laptops: remove back panel, swap the M.2 card, reconnect the two antenna leads (main/aux)
Desktops: PCIe adapter card with antenna mount
Install Intel drivers from intel.com
Connect to 5/6 GHz SSID; verify link speed in Wi-Fi status
warning: Antenna connectors are fragile — lift straight up gently. Note which lead was main vs aux.
provenance: Standard PC upgrade procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Monitor Upgrade: Resolution and Refresh
overview: The monitor is what you actually look at — and the GPU must drive it. Match the panel to the GPU: 1080p/144Hz for mid GPUs, 1440p/144Hz+ for strong ones, 4K only for flagships.

demo.how_to_run: python checker.py  — edit the YOUR BUILD section with your parts

compatibility_checks: GPU can drive the resolution/refresh in YOUR games (check benchmarks)
Cable: DisplayPort 1.4 for 1440p/144Hz+; HDMI 2.1 for 4K/120
Desk space and VESA mount if arm-mounting
Panel type: IPS (color), VA (contrast), OLED (best, burn-in care)
bottleneck_notes: A monitor "bottlenecks" what you SEE: a 60Hz panel hides a 200fps GPU. Upgrade the monitor and GPU as a pair when possible.
steps: Pick resolution/refresh your GPU sustains
Connect via DisplayPort (preferred) or HDMI 2.1
Windows: set the refresh rate (Settings > Display > Advanced) — it defaults to 60Hz!
Enable FreeSync/G-Sync in GPU control panel
Calibrate: brightness/contrast; night light as desired
warning: Remember to actually SET the refresh rate — most "144Hz not working" cases are this one toggle.
provenance: Standard PC upgrade procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Sound Card / DAC Upgrade
overview: Onboard audio is good now — upgrade only with good headphones/speakers. A USB DAC/amp beats internal sound cards for simplicity and noise isolation.

demo.how_to_run: python checker.py  — edit the YOUR BUILD section with your parts

compatibility_checks: Headphones/speakers good enough to reveal a difference
USB port free (DAC) or PCIe slot (internal card)
Impedance: high-impedance headphones need an amp
bottleneck_notes: Audio "bottlenecks" are the weakest link: a $300 DAC into $20 earbuds changes nothing. Upgrade transducers (headphones/speakers) first.
steps: Choose USB DAC/amp for simplicity
Plug in, let Windows install it
Set as default: Settings > Sound > Output
Disable onboard audio in BIOS (optional, avoids conflicts)
Test with familiar music
warning: None.
provenance: Standard PC upgrade procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Capture Card Install
overview: Capture cards record/stream consoles or second PCs without load on the gaming machine. Internal PCIe for fixed setups, USB for portability.

demo.how_to_run: python checker.py  — edit the YOUR BUILD section with your parts

compatibility_checks: PCIe x1/x4 slot (internal) or USB 3.0+ (external)
Target resolution/refresh supported (1080p60 vs 4K60)
HDMI version chain: console > card > monitor passthrough
Streaming PC specs for encoding
bottleneck_notes: Capture cards offload encoding from the gaming PC — the "bottleneck" they fix is game performance while streaming.
steps: Install card (PCIe) or plug in (USB)
Route: console HDMI out > capture card in > card out > monitor
Install vendor software (Elgato 4K Capture Utility etc.)
Add as Video Capture Device in OBS
Set resolution/fps to match; test passthrough latency
warning: HDCP-protected content (some apps) will show black — that is by design, not a fault.
provenance: Standard PC upgrade procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: BIOS/UEFI Update Safely
overview: BIOS updates add CPU support and fix bugs — but a failed flash can brick the board. Update only for a reason, never during a storm, and prefer boards with BIOS Flashback.

demo.how_to_run: python checker.py  — edit the YOUR BUILD section with your parts

compatibility_checks: New BIOS actually supports your CPU / fixes your issue (read the changelog)
Correct file for your EXACT board revision
Boards with BIOS Flashback can recover from bad flashes
bottleneck_notes: BIOS versions gate CPU support and memory compatibility — the "bottleneck" is features/stability, not speed.
steps: Check current version in BIOS or msinfo32
Download from the motherboard vendor ONLY (exact model/revision)
Read the changelog — update only if it helps you
Use the BIOS built-in flash utility (M-Flash/Q-Flash/EZ Flash), not Windows tools
Do NOT power off during the flash; use a UPS if power is flaky
Load optimized defaults after, re-enable XMP, re-check boot order
warning: A power cut mid-flash bricks most boards. Do not update "just because".
provenance: Standard PC upgrade procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Socket and Chipset Compatibility Checks
overview: The master compatibility skill: sockets are physical (pins must match), chipsets are logical (features/support). Both must agree. This guide teaches the check itself.

demo.how_to_run: python checker.py  — edit the YOUR BUILD section with your parts

compatibility_checks: Socket: CPU socket == motherboard socket (AM4/AM5/LGA1700 — no adapters exist)
Chipset: on the vendor CPU support list for your board
BIOS: version meets the minimum on the support list
RAM generation: board’s DDR type
Cooler: bracket for the socket; TDP rating
bottleneck_notes: Incompatible parts do not "bottleneck" — they do not work at all. This check prevents the most expensive beginner mistake.
steps: Write down: motherboard exact model, current BIOS, RAM type
Open the vendor CPU support list page for your board
Filter by socket; confirm your target CPU is listed with a BIOS version
Check your BIOS meets it — update first if not
Run the checker below with your parts; fix every ERROR before buying
warning: Third-party "compatibility checker" sites are hints, not guarantees — the vendor list is truth.
provenance: Standard PC upgrade procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

t: Bottleneck Analysis: Find the Real Limit
title: Bottleneck Analysis: Find the Real Limit
overview: Upgrading the wrong part wastes money. Bottleneck analysis finds the actual limiter: monitor CPU vs GPU usage in YOUR workload, then upgrade the part at 100% while the other idles.

demo.how_to_run: python checker.py  — edit the YOUR BUILD section with your parts

compatibility_checks: Monitoring tools installed (MSI Afterburner + RTSS, HWiNFO64)
Test in YOUR actual games/apps, not synthetic benchmarks alone
Check at YOUR resolution — bottlenecks shift with resolution
bottleneck_notes: Rules of thumb: GPU 95-100% + CPU low = GPU-bound (upgrade GPU). CPU 100% + GPU low = CPU-bound (upgrade CPU). RAM full + disk thrash = RAM. Disk 100% = storage.
steps: Install MSI Afterburner overlay: show CPU%, GPU%, RAM, temps
Run your typical workload 10 minutes
Read the limiter: which part pins at/near 100%?
Upgrade THAT part first
Re-test: the bottleneck should move to another part (diminishing returns = balanced)
warning: Bottleneck calculators online are rough estimates — measured data beats them.
provenance: Standard PC upgrade procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Power Budget Calculator
overview: Size the PSU from real numbers: CPU TDP + GPU TDP + 150W system, times 1.4 for headroom. This guide plus the checker below does the math.

demo.how_to_run: python checker.py  — edit the YOUR BUILD section with your parts

compatibility_checks: Real TDPs from vendor specs (not marketing)
Transient spikes: high-end GPUs spike above TDP — headroom covers it
12V rail capacity matters more than total watts on old units
Efficiency rating: Gold+ wastes less as heat
bottleneck_notes: An undersized PSU does not slow the PC — it crashes it. "Bottleneck" here means stability ceiling.
steps: List every part’s TDP (CPU, GPU from vendor pages)
Add 150W for board/RAM/drives/fans
Multiply by 1.4 for headroom and capacitor aging
Round UP to the next standard size (550/650/750/850)
Buy 80+ Gold from a reputable brand with long warranty
warning: Cheap no-name PSUs lie about wattage — buy reputable or do not buy.
provenance: Standard PC upgrade procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

t: Adding a Second Drive / Dual Boot
title: Adding a Second Drive / Dual Boot
overview: A second drive is the cleanest upgrade: more space, or a second OS, without touching the working install. The only real skill is BIOS boot order.

demo.how_to_run: python checker.py  — edit the YOUR BUILD section with your parts

compatibility_checks: Free SATA port or M.2 slot
SATA power lead or M.2 standoff
GPT vs MBR: match the existing install style for dual boot
Backup before partitioning anything
bottleneck_notes: Second drives fix capacity bottlenecks, not speed — unless you move the OS to the faster drive.
steps: Install the drive (SATA cables or M.2 screw)
BIOS: confirm it appears
Windows: Disk Management > Initialize (GPT) > New Simple Volume
Dual boot Linux: shrink Windows volume first, install Linux into free space, let GRUB handle the menu
Set default OS and timeout in BIOS/GRUB
warning: Back up before resizing partitions. Install Windows BEFORE Linux for the easiest dual boot.
provenance: Standard PC upgrade procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: eGPU for Laptops
overview: External GPUs via Thunderbolt give laptops desktop graphics at a desk. Check: Thunderbolt 3/4 port (USB-C alone is NOT enough), enclosure + card cost, and ~10-20% performance loss vs internal.

demo.how_to_run: python checker.py  — edit the YOUR BUILD section with your parts

compatibility_checks: Thunderbolt 3 or 4 port REQUIRED (lightning icon)
Enclosure wattage covers the card
Card length fits the enclosure
Internal display costs more performance than external monitor
bottleneck_notes: Thunderbolt bandwidth caps eGPU scaling — beyond mid-high cards, returns diminish. Best value: mid-range card + external monitor.
steps: Confirm Thunderbolt (not just USB-C) in laptop specs
Buy enclosure + GPU; check enclosure PSU wattage
Seat card in enclosure, connect power
Thunderbolt cable to laptop; approve the device
Install GPU drivers; connect monitor to the eGPU for best performance
Undock safely via Thunderbolt software
warning: USB-C ports without Thunderbolt will NOT work — verify the lightning symbol.
provenance: Standard PC upgrade procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: External SSD Setup
overview: External SSDs over USB 3.x are fast, silent bulk storage and the easiest "upgrade" — no case opening. Match the enclosure to the drive and the port.

demo.how_to_run: python checker.py  — edit the YOUR BUILD section with your parts

compatibility_checks: USB 3.0+ port (blue/SS mark) — USB 2.0 strangles SSDs
Enclosure interface matches drive (SATA vs NVMe M.2)
UASP support for full speed
exFAT for cross-OS, NTFS for Windows-only
bottleneck_notes: External SSDs fix portability/capacity needs; the USB link caps speed below internal NVMe.
steps: Buy enclosure matching your M.2/SATA drive (or a ready-made portable SSD)
Assemble (one screw usually)
Plug into a USB 3.x port
Format exFAT (cross-platform) or NTFS
Verify speed with CrystalDiskMark; safely eject via taskbar icon
warning: Always eject before unplugging — cached writes corrupt drives.
provenance: Standard PC upgrade procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Cable Management and PSU Shrouds
overview: Tidy cables are not vanity: they unblock airflow, make future upgrades easy, and stop fans eating loose wires. Route behind the tray, group with ties.

demo.how_to_run: python checker.py  — edit the YOUR BUILD section with your parts

compatibility_checks: Case has behind-tray routing space
Modular PSU helps enormously
Enough cable length to route around, not across
bottleneck_notes: Cable clutter "bottlenecks" airflow and your own future upgrade speed.
steps: Power off, unplug
Route 24-pin, CPU 8-pin, PCIe behind the motherboard tray
Group with velcro ties (not zip ties — reusable)
Keep cables clear of all fan blades
Front-panel connectors last (use the manual diagram)
Power on; verify all fans spin freely
warning: A cable in a fan blade stops the fan — check clearances before closing up.
provenance: Standard PC upgrade procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Post-Upgrade Benchmarking
overview: Prove the upgrade worked: benchmark before and after with the same tests. Numbers beat feelings — and they catch problems (like XMP left off) early.

demo.how_to_run: python checker.py  — edit the YOUR BUILD section with your parts

compatibility_checks: Same benchmark versions before/after
Same driver/settings for fair comparison
Temps logged alongside scores
bottleneck_notes: Post-upgrade benchmarks reveal the NEW bottleneck — upgrades move the limit, they rarely remove it.

Upgrade
After: enable XMP, install drivers, re-run identical tests
Compare: big gains where expected? If not, investigate (seating, drivers, XMP)
Log final numbers in your build notes

title: Selling or Donating Old Parts
overview: Old parts fund new ones — if you wipe and test them honestly. Data destruction on drives is non-negotiable; everything else is clean, photograph, and describe accurately.

demo.how_to_run: python checker.py  — edit the YOUR BUILD section with your parts

compatibility_checks: Part works (test before listing)
Drives: secure erase / full format — personal data must be unrecoverable
Include original accessories if you have them
bottleneck_notes: N/A — but selling the old GPU/CPU often funds half the upgrade.
steps: SSDs/HDDs: secure erase (vendor tool) or full format; then reinstall nothing
Clean dust; photograph actual item, not stock photos
List with exact model, condition, and reason for sale
Price from recently SOLD listings, not asking prices
Donate working old PCs to schools/nonprofits (wiped!) for goodwill
warning: A quick format does NOT erase data — use secure erase or full (not quick) format.
provenance: Standard PC upgrade procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.

title: Upgrade Priority Decision Tree
overview: The master decision guide: answer what feels slow, check the bottleneck, and the tree tells you which upgrade buys the most speed per dollar for YOUR system.

demo.how_to_run: python checker.py  — edit the YOUR BUILD section with your parts

compatibility_checks: Bottleneck measured (see Bottleneck Analysis guide)
Budget set
Current parts inventoried (CPU-Z + checker below)
bottleneck_notes: Priority order for most old PCs: 1) SSD if still on HDD, 2) RAM to 16 GB if swapping, 3) GPU if gaming and GPU-bound, 4) CPU/platform if CPU-bound, 5) PSU if wattage insufficient, 6) monitor to see the gains.
steps: Measure: what is slow, and which part pins at 100%? (Afterburner overlay)
If HDD system drive: SSD first — always
If RAM swapping: RAM to 16 GB
If GPU-bound in games: GPU (check PSU + case fit)
If CPU-bound: CPU (check socket/chipset/BIOS)
If PSU undersized for planned GPU: PSU with the GPU
Re-measure after each upgrade
warning: Never buy parts before the compatibility checks pass — measure twice, buy once.
provenance: Standard PC upgrade procedure; fact-checked against vendor documentation.
